extracted.intended_audience: public relations students and practitioners (including investor-relations and lobbyists)
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and regulatory standards public relations practitioners must follow when producing communications (press releases, advertising, lobbying materials, investor relations disclosures, internships, etc.). Covers U.S. statutes and rules (BCRA, Lobbying Disclosure Act, FARA, SEC acts, copyright, trademark, libel/privacy, labor law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Electioneering communications rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio or television advertising that refers to a federal candidate and is made within 60 days of a general election and within 30 days of a primary is an 'electioneering communication.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations, trade associations, and labor unions may only run 'electioneering communications' through their PACs, using hard money contributions. Any entity making 'electioneering communications' must file a disclosure report with the FEC listing those who gave more than $1,000 for the communication and those who received more than $200 relative to the advertisement.

rubrics_metrics.name: BCRA principal provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Main provisions of the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act (BCRA) are 'soft money' prohibitions, increases in contribution limits, and limits on 'electioneering communications' (commercials that support or oppose a candidate without explicitly urging that candidate’s election or defeat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbyist definition (Lobbying Disclosure Act)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lobbyist is someone employed or retained by a client who makes more than one contact on behalf of that client and spends at least 20 percent of her/his time during a six-month period providing that service to the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition determines who must register and file reports under federal lobbying laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying firm and lobbying contact definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: A lobbying firm is an entity that has at least one person who was hired to represent someone other than her/his employer (including self-employed individuals who represent others). A lobbying contact is defined as a communication, either oral or written, on behalf of a client to a covered executive or legislative branch official regarding legislation, rules, regulations, grants, loans, permits, programs, or nominations.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as lobbying vs. excluded activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbying includes direct pressure on members of Congress (including 'artificially stimulated letter writing campaigns'), but does not include general public relations campaigns designed to sway public opinion and activate constituents (so-called 'grassroots lobbying'), testimony before an invited committee of Congress, or ordinary news items and editorials by magazines and newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The distinction hinges on whether communication is 'direct' contact with government officials. Grassroots activity is part of First Amendment rights and is not the type of lobbying that requires registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbying registration and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Lobbyists and lobbying firms must register with the Secretary of the Senate and the Clerk of the House and must report names, addresses, places of business, and phone numbers of their own business, their clients, and anyone else who contributes more than $10,000 in a six-month period to lobbying activities conducted by the registrant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All registrants must file reports twice a year, providing 'good faith estimates' of the amounts paid by clients or spent on lobbying. Lobbying laws also apply to nonprofit charitable, educational, and other tax-exempt organizations; nonprofits that engage in lobbying are prohibited from receiving federal grants, awards, contracts, and loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All public relations practitioners working for 'foreign principals' must register under FARA within 10 days with the U.S. Attorney General, whether or not they lobby U.S. government officials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FARA defines a 'foreign agent' as anyone in the United States who works as a 'public relations counsel, publicity agent, information service employee, or political consultant,' acting at the direction of a foreign principal. Information materials produced by foreign agents (communications designed to influence the American public about political interests or policies of a foreign government, to influence U.S. foreign policy, to promote tensions, or to advocate overthrow) must be labeled as 'political propaganda' and copies must be provided to the U.S. Attorney General.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noncompete clause enforceability tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Most contractual noncompete agreements fail to meet one or more of three tests: they must be reasonable in scope; supported by some monetary consideration; and protect only the employer’s legitimate business interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a noncompete is broader than necessary, lacks consideration, or protects purposes unrelated to legitimate business interests (e.g., elimination of competition), courts are likely not to uphold it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six criteria for legal internships (must meet all six)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exhibit 6.4 lists six criteria: (1) The internship is similar to training given in an educational environment; (2) The internship experience is for the benefit of the intern; (3) The intern does not displace regular employees and works under close supervision; (4) The employer derives no immediate advantage and operations may be impeded; (5) The intern is not necessarily entitled to a job at conclusion; (6) Employer and intern understand the intern is not entitled to wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The internship must meet all six requirements; if it does not, the position should be treated as a regular employee entitled to minimum wage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright basics and eligible categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright subsists in 'original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression.' The eight categories include literary works (databases, computer programs, textbooks), musical works, dramatic works, pictorial/graphic/sculptural works, motion pictures and audiovisual works, sound recordings, and architectural works created after 1990.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public domain status occurs when copyright has expired, when an author never claimed copyright, or when materials were produced by government employees on government-paid time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright notice and registration requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A copyright exists automatically when a work is created and copyright notice is placed on the work. The copyright notice must have three elements: (1) the word 'Copyright' or abbreviation 'Copr.' or symbol ©; (2) the year of first publication; and (3) the name of the copyright owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal registration is necessary for a copyright owner to bring suit for infringement, but registration can be made after infringement has occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-for-hire and freelancer ownership rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Who owns copyright when an individual completes a 'work for hire' depends on two statutory definitions: works made by an employee as part of employment (copyright belongs to employer) and certain specially ordered/commissioned works where ownership depends on whether the creator is an employee or independent contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freelancers who want to retain copyright for work produced as a 'work for hire' must have a written agreement signed by all parties specifying ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The following factors determine fair use: purpose and character of the use (commercial or nonprofit educational), nature of the copyrighted work, amount and substantiality of the portion used, and effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 6.1 gives practical permission guidelines (when to seek permission vs. generally not required), but decisions depend on balancing these four factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof elements for copyright infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove infringement, the copyright owner must show originality of the work, probable access by the infringer, and substantial similarity of the unauthorized work to the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent case law (e.g., file-sharing software developers) shows liability may extend to developers for end-user infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark creation, registration process, and duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark rights are created through adoption and use in trade; registration with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office creates presumptions of ownership. Formal application includes a drawing, filing fee, and three examples of use. The ® symbol indicates completed registration; 'TM' is used when registration is pending for a mark identifying a product and 'SM' for a service mark. Completed registration lasts 10 years with 10-year renewals as long as the mark is used in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply for registration after confirming no other party has registered the name/phrase/logo (often via commercial research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark enforcement standards and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark enforcement is limited to situations with a likelihood of confusion or deception, or where use would tarnish or dilute the mark's value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful infringement suits may recover treble damages (three times the infringer's profits or damages, whichever greater) plus reasonable attorney's fees, and infringing materials 'shall be delivered up and destroyed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark usage/style guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners remind journalists and PR practitioners to use trademarks as adjectives, not nouns or verbs, and to use capital letters when referring to products (e.g., say 'a Xerox photocopier' but do not 'Xerox' a document).

rubrics_metrics.name: Investor-relations disclosure for securities offerings (Securities Act of 1933)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Securities Act of 1933 restricts corporate communication before and during the period that new securities offerings are being registered and requires filings with the SEC when securities are offered to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must provide 'material information' about new security offerings so that investors can make purchasing decisions based on facts; 'material' means likely to have a significant effect on securities prices or important to a reasonable investor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic reporting and integrated disclosure (Securities Exchange Act of 1934)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 regulates trading after initial distribution and requires periodic reporting about a company; it also created the SEC to enforce securities laws and protect investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the SEC’s 'integrated disclosure system,' corporations with public shareholders must continuously provide information that affects stockholders' understanding of the financial position and prospects of a company; practitioners must issue press releases, draft speeches, and write quarterly and annual reports to achieve 'adequate and accurate information.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe Harbor for forward-looking statements (PSLRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 created a 'Safe Harbor for Forward-Looking Statements' to encourage dissemination of forecasts without fear of litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies may be protected from liability for predictions about earnings and performance as long as such forecasts are tempered by 'meaningful' cautionary statements explaining why projections might fail to come true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate disclosure procedures for material information
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate disclosure depends on company size and shareholder dispersion, but exchanges may require, 'at a minimum,' simultaneous release of material announcements to national business and financial news wire services, national news wire services, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, Moody’s, and Standard & Poor’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic principle—public statements must be truthful; simply issuing a news release may not be sufficient to fulfill disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insider trading, tipping prohibitions, and compliance updates (Sarbanes–Oxley)
rubrics_metrics.description: Securities regulations prohibit fraud in trading (insiders using nonpublic information or 'tipping' others). 'Insiders' include corporate executives, public relations personnel, outside accountants, lawyers, outside PR counsel, and other professionals with access to corporate plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New legislation (Sarbanes–Oxley Act of 2002) and SEC/NYSE rules increase transparency, hold top management accountable for financial reports, and further ensure insiders cannot exercise unfair advantage in compensation or stock trading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation (libel/slander) core elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Key elements of a libel action include: Defamation (communication that injures reputation), Identification (language 'of or concerning' the plaintiff), Publication (witnessed by a third party), Fault (degree of mistake), Falsity, and Damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication can occur via brochures, newsletters, fiction, yard signs, memos, conversations, emails, and websites; anyone who repeats the libelous statement can also be sued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of fault and burdens by plaintiff type (New York Times v. Sullivan and Gertz)
rubrics_metrics.description: Public officials must prove 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth). Public figures are treated like public officials for higher scrutiny; private figures generally prove negligence (failure to act as a 'reasonable person').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Falsity standards generally apply to public officials/figures. Damages: compensatory (actual financial harms) and punitive (non-financial harms; punitive damages require proof of actual malice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural defenses, statutes of limitations, and practical considerations in libel suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible defenses/outcomes include summary judgment for the defendant if the plaintiff fails to meet the burden of proof, or dismissal for exceeding the statute of limitations (varying by state, generally one to three years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before suing, corporations/executives should weigh public-opinion ramifications; PR practitioners must remind thin-skinned executives that First Amendment protections may shield caustic or false public discussion in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy torts and state law variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy is an individual's right 'to be let alone.' Defamation and privacy violations are 'torts' and state tort law varies, so practitioners must know and understand state-specific libel and privacy rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners can use free online legal information services (e.g., findlaw.com) to begin researching applicability of state laws.
